title: Hepatitis B and C Management in 2025: Guideline-Driven, Elimination-Focused Care
summary: In 2025, chronic hepatitis B (CHB) management is shifting toward broader treatment eligibility to reduce morbidity and transmission, while hepatitis C (HCV) management emphasizes simplified, universal DAA treatment with short, highly effective pangenotypic regimens. Policies align with elimination goals, prioritizing test-and-treat models, decentralized delivery, and attention to high-risk populations.
clinicalQuestion: What are the 2025 best practices for screening, treatment initiation, antiviral selection, monitoring, and public health priorities for hepatitis B and C?

heroStats.label: Strategic goal
heroStats.value: ≥20% reduction in new HCV infections by 2025 [6], [7], [10]

heroStats.label: HBV treatment trend
heroStats.value: Movement to expand therapy beyond classic ALT/DNA thresholds [1], [14]

keyMoments.title: Simplified HCV regimens for all adults
keyMoments.body: WHO-backed pangenotypic options for 8–12 weeks with **SVR ≥94–95%** enable scale-up in primary care and community settings [2], [5], [8].

keyMoments.title: CHB thresholds are evolving
keyMoments.body: 2025 expert discussions and guideline updates support **broader CHB treatment**, including persons in the ‘indeterminate/grey zone’ and special populations to curb progression and transmission [1], [11], [12], [13], [14].

keyMoments.title: Prevention and elimination alignment
keyMoments.body: CDC national progress reports target **≥20% reduction in incident HCV** and stress surveillance, linkage-to-care, and harm reduction integration [6], [7], [10].

keyMoments.title: Beyond the liver: extrahepatic gains
keyMoments.body: Successful DAA therapy is associated with **reduced extrahepatic manifestations** risk, reinforcing treatment for all eligible HCV patients [9].

sections.title: Screening and Initial Evaluation (HBV and HCV)
sections.blurb: Prioritize universal, once-in-a-lifetime testing in adults with opt-out reflex pathways; repeat based on risk. Integrate vaccination and harm reduction.

steps.title: HBV: Who to test and what to obtain
steps.body: Use HBsAg, anti-HBs, and anti-HBc (total or IgG) with reflex HBeAg, anti-HBe, and quantitative HBV DNA for those HBsAg positive. Baseline ALT/AST, bilirubin, albumin, INR, platelet count, fibrosis staging (transient elastography preferred), and HDV screening in HBsAg-positive individuals. 2025 updates emphasize broader screening and routine HDV assessment in HBsAg-positive patients [11], [12], [13].

steps.title: HCV: Who to test and what to obtain
steps.body: Adopt universal, one-time anti-HCV testing with reflex HCV RNA; repeat testing for ongoing risk (e.g., injection drug use, high-risk exposures). Baseline labs include ALT/AST, bilirubin, platelet count, eGFR, HIV, HBV serologies (vaccinate non-immune), pregnancy testing when relevant, and noninvasive fibrosis staging. Streamlined pathways support same-day treatment starts where feasible [2], [4], [7].

steps.title: Vaccination and prevention
steps.body: Offer HBV vaccination to all non-immune, including those with HCV. Counsel on harm reduction, sterile injection supplies, and naloxone distribution; integrate opioid use disorder treatment. These measures align with national reduction targets for incident HCV [6], [7], [10].

sections.title: When to Start, What to Use, and How to Monitor (2025)
sections.blurb: Guidelines increasingly support earlier treatment to reduce progression and transmission while tailoring to fibrosis and special populations.

cards.title: Initiation signals
items: Classic criteria: elevated ALT with high HBV DNA or significant fibrosis/cirrhosis.
2025 perspective: consider treatment in the **indeterminate/grey zone**, particularly with age >30–35, family history of HCC, or fluctuating ALT/DNA [1], [11], [13], [14].
Treat all with cirrhosis and detectable HBV DNA regardless of ALT; treat if on immunosuppression or chemotherapy.
Screen and treat HBV in pregnancy if **HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL** to prevent MTCT; use tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) in late pregnancy per evolving practice patterns [11], [13].

cards.title: First-line antivirals
items: **Tenofovir (TDF or TAF)** and **entecavir** are preferred for potency and high barrier to resistance.
TAF is favored when renal dysfunction or bone disease risk exists; entecavir requires consideration of prior lamivudine resistance.
Pegylated interferon has niche use; most adults use nucleos(t)ide analogues [11], [13].

cards.title: Targets and outcomes
items: Primary: sustained HBV DNA suppression to undetectable; ALT normalization; fibrosis stabilization or regression.
HBeAg-positive: aim for HBeAg seroconversion with confirmed DNA suppression.
HBsAg loss remains uncommon; therapy is generally long-term or indefinite in most non-cirrhotic adults.

cards.title: Monitoring
items: Every 3–6 months: ALT/AST, HBV DNA; HBeAg/anti-HBe as indicated; adherence assessment.
Renal function and phosphate with TDF; bone health in at-risk patients.
HCC surveillance with ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months in at-risk groups (all with cirrhosis; non-cirrhotic with high-risk demographics/family history).

cards.title: Special populations
items: Pregnancy: antiviral prophylaxis if high DNA; neonatal HBV vaccine + HBIG at birth.
Coinfections (HIV/HDV/HCV): coordinate regimens; screen all HBsAg-positive for HDV per 2025 updates [11], [12], [13].
Immunosuppression: prophylaxis for HBsAg-positive and selected anti-HBc–positive individuals to prevent reactivation.

sections.title: Simplified Treatment and Delivery in 2025
sections.blurb: Short-course pangenotypic DAAs achieve very high cure rates; prioritize test-and-treat models and outreach in high-incidence settings.

cards.title: Who to treat
items: Treat all adults and adolescents with chronic HCV unless life expectancy is too short to benefit.
People who use or inject drugs should be offered treatment without delay; outcomes are excellent with supportive services [2], [4].
Acute HCV: treat upon diagnosis to reduce transmission and accelerate elimination programs [2].

cards.title: First-line DAA regimens
items: WHO-endorsed options include two to three **pangenotypic combinations** for **8–12 weeks**, delivering **SVR ≥94–95%** across populations [2], [5], [8].
Choice depends on cirrhosis status, prior therapy, drug–drug interactions, and renal function.
No head-to-head randomized trials show superiority among the leading regimens as of 2025 [2].

cards.title: Pretreatment essentials
items: Confirm viremia with HCV RNA; stage fibrosis noninvasively to identify cirrhosis.
Review concomitant medications for interactions; check pregnancy status when applicable.
Screen for HBV and vaccinate if non-immune; counsel on reinfection risk and prevention.

cards.title: Effectiveness and broader benefits
items: **SVR12 ≥94–95%** with contemporary DAAs in routine practice [5], [8].
DAA cure is associated with lower risk of **extrahepatic manifestations** (e.g., mixed cryoglobulinemia, certain lymphomas) [9].
Cirrhotics require continued HCC surveillance post-cure.

cards.title: Models of care and access
items: Deliver DAAs in primary care, opioid treatment programs, and syringe services; onsite initiation improves uptake [4].
Decentralized, same-day start pathways reduce loss to follow-up and support elimination targets [2], [7], [10].
Align local programs with CDC’s 2025 reduction benchmarks and surveillance improvement [6], [7], [10].
